moments.title: Two correlation coefficients
moments.text: Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient $r$, and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient $r_s$.

moments.title: Is the trend strong?
moments.text: A line of best fit shows a trend; correlation measures how strong it is.

moments.title: Direction
moments.text: Positive: $y$ rises as $x$ rises. Negative: $y$ falls, as with coffee sales on hotter days.

moments.title: Strength
moments.text: Strength is how close the points lie to the line: strong, moderate, or weak.

moments.title: Rough bands for $r$
moments.text: A rule of thumb: about 0.75 to 1 strong, 0.5 to 0.75 moderate, 0.1 to 0.5 weak; the same for negative values.

moments.title: Finding $r$
moments.text: Enter $x$ and $y$ as two lists and run a two-variable statistics calculation (TI-Nspire shown).

moments.title: $r=0.854$
moments.text: Strong positive correlation between years of teaching and performance score.

moments.title: Spearman's $r_s$
moments.text: The same correlation calculation, but on the ranks of the data instead of the values.

moments.title: Ranking
moments.text: Rank each variable from 1 to 8. Either direction works, as long as both variables use the same one.

moments.title: Plotting the ranks
moments.text: Rank against rank: not a perfect 1-1, 2-2 pattern, but close.

moments.title: $r_s=0.814$
moments.text: Enter the ranks as the data and repeat the two-variable calculation.

notes.title: Tied values
notes.text: The example has no tied values, so the video does not show how to rank them.
notes.write: Give tied values the average of the ranks they would take, for example 5.5 and 5.5.

ican.text: I can rank two variables in the same direction and average the ranks of tied values.
I can find $r_s$ on my GDC by finding $r$ for the two lists of ranks.
I can interpret $r_s$ in context, as an association between the ranks.
I can give a mathematical reason to choose $r_s$ over $r$, or $r$ over $r_s$.
I can decide whether changing one data value changes $r_s$.

ku.text: Spearman's $r_s$ is Pearson's $r$ calculated on the ranks of the data instead of the values.
$r_s$ measures how monotonic a relationship is: whether $y$ always rises (or always falls) as $x$ rises, straight line or not.
Tied values share the average of the ranks they would take. Two values tied for 5th and 6th both get rank 5.5.
$r_s$ is less sensitive to outliers than $r$, because an extreme value can only move to the end of the ranking.
Changing a value without changing its rank leaves $r_s$ unchanged.
Use $r$ for a linear relationship between measurements. Use $r_s$ for ranked data, a curved but monotonic pattern, or data with outliers.

visuals.text: The typing data: a curved, decreasing scatter. Caption: $r=-0.899$ but $r_s=-0.994$; the pattern is monotonic, not linear.
The same scatter plotted as rank against rank. Caption: ranking straightens a monotonic pattern.
One point dragged far out as an outlier, with $r$ and $r_s$ before and after. Caption: $r$ moves a lot, $r_s$ barely moves.

misc.weak: "$r_s=-0.994$, so there is a strong negative linear correlation between practice hours and errors."
misc.better: $r_s=-0.994$ shows a strong negative association between the ranks: students who practise more tend to make fewer errors.
misc.evidence: Markschemes have refused interpretations that are not stated in terms of the ranks, and have said "strong positive" alone is not enough.

misc.weak: Giving two tied values the same lower rank (both 5), then carrying on from 6.
misc.better: Average the ranks they would take: both get 5.5, and the next value is 7.
misc.evidence: Syllabus guidance: if data items are equal, ranks are averaged.

misc.weak: Ranking one variable from largest to smallest and the other from smallest to largest.
misc.better: Rank both variables in the same direction. Reversing one ranking flips the sign of $r_s$.
misc.evidence: Reversing only one ranking gives the wrong sign, and markschemes take a mark off for a missing negative sign.

misc.better: An outlier changes $r_s$ only through its rank, so $r_s$ is less affected than $r$.
misc.evidence: Syllabus guidance; also credited as a reason for choosing Spearman's.

terms.text: Fill in the ranks as given in the table layout; ties averaged.
Name both variables, the direction, and refer to their ranks.
One mathematical reason, such as non-linear pattern or an outlier, tied to these data.

formula.text: Nothing for this code is in the formula booklet. Find $r_s$ with the GDC.

gdc.text: Rank both variables by hand, averaging ties. Enter the ranks in List 3 and List 4.
[F2] CALC, [F6] SET: 2Var XList = List3, 2Var YList = List4, [EXIT].
[F3] REG, [F1] X, [F1] ax+b. The value of $r$ shown is $r_s$.
The fx-CG50 has no built-in Spearman's function, so ranking is always by hand.
Put back: set 2Var XList = List1 and 2Var YList = List2.

worked.prompt: A typing teacher records the hours of practice, $h$, and the number of errors, $E$, in a test for eight students.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Rank both variables from smallest to largest.

parts.label: (c)
parts.a: Strong negative association between the ranks: students who practise more tend to make fewer errors.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Pearson's $r$ for these data is $-0.899$. Suggest why $r_s$ is the better measure here.
parts.a: The errors fall quickly at first and then level off, so the pattern is curved but always decreasing. $r_s$ measures a monotonic relationship; $r$ only a linear one.

kq.q: The top score in a data set is lowered by 20, but it is still the top score. Why does $r_s$ not change?
kq.model: $r_s$ depends only on the ranks. The value changed, but its rank did not, so every rank and $r_s$ stay the same.
Any relationship that always increases but is curved, such as $y=x^2$ for positive $x$. The ranks match perfectly, but the points are not on a straight line.

kq.q: Why does a U-shaped relationship give $r_s$ close to 0?
kq.model: The pattern falls then rises, so it is not monotonic. High ranks of $x$ pair with both high and low ranks of $y$, and the effect cancels.

history.text: Charles Spearman, an English psychologist, introduced his rank method in 1904 in "The proof and measurement of association between two things", written while he was still a graduate student. The same year he published his theory of general intelligence.
sources: Spearman (1904), American Journal of Psychology 15(1), doi:10.2307/1412159

explorers.name: Pearson versus Spearman
explorers.spec: Students click to add or drag points. The page shows $r$ and $r_s$ live. A Linear toggle draws the line of best fit. A Monotonic toggle joins the points in $x$ order and labels the pattern increasing, decreasing, or neither.
explorers.suggest: Optionally show the rank table beside the plot, so students see that dragging a point without passing a neighbour leaves $r_s$ unchanged.

config.intro: Click the grid to add a point; drag a point to move it. Compare Pearson's $r$, which measures a straight line, with Spearman's $r_s$, which only asks whether the pattern always rises or always falls.

presets.label: Linear
presets.story: A straight-line pattern: $r$ and $r_s$ are both close to 1.

presets.label: Curved
presets.story: Hours of typing practice (across) and errors in a test (up), as on the SL 4.10 worked example. Always decreasing, but curved.

presets.label: Outlier
presets.story: Seven points on a rising line and one extreme point. $r$ drops because the point is far from the line; $r_s$ stays at 1 because the point is still ranked last. Drag it below its neighbours and watch $r_s$ move.

presets.label: U shape
presets.story: Falls, then rises. Neither coefficient sees this pattern.
